title: Trump’s Iran headaches are mounting
description: The Iran war hasn’t gone well for President Donald Trump since, well, shortly after it began.
fullText:
The Iran war hasn't gone well for President Donald Trump since, well, shortly after it began.

Despite extensive US military attacks and economic pressure, Iran hasn't felt the need to capitulate to Trump's demands. And even when there have been ceasefires with favorable terms for Iran, Tehran still didn't abide by them.

But Trump's headaches with the war are mounting. And many of them extend beyond the battlefield and the negotiating table.

Some of the recent developments:

Trump's newly reported secret plane switch in Turkey due to a potential Iranian threat is raising major questions about the administration using staff and media as decoys. The revelation is also undercutting the administration's claims about Iran's diminished capabilities and leading to mockery of Trump, including by Iranian state media.

The United States' munitions shortfall problem — which Trump was warned about before the war began — appears to be coming to a head.

There are increasing signs of Trump administration officials and allies growing weary of the war and looking for or urging an off-ramp.

There are now also increasing reports of declining living conditions and mental health aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln amid an extraordinarily long deployment to support the war effort. CNN reported Thursday that one sailor went overboard wearing a life vest, with a US official saying the Navy viewed the event as a "mental health" incident.

And through it all, Iran only appears to be growing bolder and upping its demands — perhaps believing that its leverage is increasing.

All of the above threatens Trump's ability to keep prosecuting the war. And these developments add to the costs of a war — now in its sixth month — whose purpose Americans have never been convinced of in the first place. The president insists he's not feeling the time pressure, but some in his party would beg to differ with the midterms looming.

The plane switch in particular threatens to add a layer of scandal over the already unpopular war. And as much as anything, it undercuts the administration's claims to have decimated Iran militarily.

This week we learned that the Trump administration feared a threat from Iran was serious enough that it warranted sneaking the president off Air Force One for his departure from Turkey last month. (CNN reported Wednesday that the threat involved a shoulder-fired missile.)

The munitions supply has long been a sleeping giant. CNN has reported that Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and other military leaders warned Trump before the war began that the stockpiles could be an issue in a protracted conflict.

Trump seemed to anticipate a much shorter war, lasting four to six weeks or so. But that's not what he's gotten. And increasing reports, including from CNN, suggest Caine's warnings were well-founded and that key munitions are significantly depleted. The US military has exhausted nearly 80% of its interceptors for a key missile defense system, known as THAAD.

The Trump administration has claimed it has plenty of munitions to finish the job in Iran. But that doesn't address whether the war might cause the US to be so short of critical munitions — which take time to replenish — that it leaves the country exposed or might embolden an adversary like China to try and invade Taiwan.

That's increasingly a cost-benefit analysis that administration officials will need to consider. But it's already a dynamic that threatens Trump's ability to apply pressure on Iran.

A major question, of course, is whether military or administration officials could even prevail upon Trump if they regard the munitions issue as being dire. But there are increasing signs that key figures are growing weary of the war and sending signals that it might be time to ramp it up.

CNN reported last week that Caine has privately made clear to other top Trump advisers that the administration needs to find an off-ramp from the war because the military options on the table to escalate the conflict could backfire, and airpower alone is unlikely to achieve Trump's objectives.

There are also signs that loyal Trump allies are increasingly concerned about the war costing Republicans in the 2026 midterm elections. House Speaker Mike Johnson said recently that "we've got to wrap it up," and Fox News host Laura Ingraham has said the "clock is ticking." (Indeed, the Guardian recently reported that more Iran war skepticism is seeping in on the normally rah-rah airwaves of Fox.) Even cheerleaders for Trump and his war effort like right-wing influencer Benny Johnson have signaled it's time to move on.

"Foreign wars with no end in sight are always unpopular. They will always be political cancer," Johnson posted on X two weeks ago. He added: "End the war. Be done. Refocus on America. Gas, grocery, home prices and immigration. Thats how we win."

The length of the war also appears to be contributing to another problem for the administration's ability to keep prosecuting it: fatigue, poor living conditions and declining mental health among the service members tasked with supporting the war effort.

News outlets Stars and Stripes and the Navy Times have reported multiple attempts by crew members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln to jump overboard. A sailor recently went overboard, CNN reported, before being rescued.

And around 200 family members of Lincoln crew members voiced concerns about the situation — including lack of supplies, food shortages and water contamination — at town halls last week in San Diego. The Lincoln has been deployed since November and hasn't made a port call in more than 200 days, which Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said is a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea.

The US Navy said it takes "every service member's well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise."

But the emerging story epitomizes Trump's problems.

He seems to regard continuing the war and keeping up the economic pressure on Iran as largely a cost-free endeavor. The US doesn't have boots on the ground and there aren't constant stories about troop deaths. Rising gas prices have been the war's biggest political problem.

But as the situation stretches months beyond when the administration signaled it would end, other problems are seeping in. Some of them make continuing the war more difficult on a practical level, while others suggest the stalemate will keep giving the administration political problems that it — and its allies — have to reckon with.

And given the war was already looking like an albatross and a quagmire – with the midterms less than three months away — these are pretty inauspicious developments.

title: Afghanistan marks 5 years under the Taliban with safer streets but pleas for jobs and education
description: As Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers mark five years since sweeping back to power, some Kabul residents say they feel safer after decades of conflict and upheaval but stress the leaders should now focus on...
fullText:
KABUL, Afghanistan (AP) — As Afghanistan's Taliban rulers mark five years since sweeping back to power, some Kabul residents say they feel safer after decades of conflict and upheaval but stress the leaders should now focus on creating jobs and expanding access to schools in the country where girls above the age of 12 are banned from education.

The Taliban regained control of Afghanistan on Aug. 15, 2021, after it launched an offensive as the U.S. and other NATO troops withdrew from the country after two decades of war. The withdrawal led to chaotic scenes at and around Kabul's airport with thousands wanting to leave.

"Thank God, the past five years have passed in safety," said Mohammad Qasim, 30, reflecting on the anniversary that comes against a backdrop of economic hardship in a conflict-stricken country. "Our wish and hope from the government is to create job opportunities for the youth."

"We, along with the entire nation, call upon the government to create employment opportunities for the youth and to encourage them to pursue education," he added.

Before the takeover, the Taliban stated that, upon assuming power, it would allow women access to education, employment and public participation, albeit in accordance with its interpretation of Islamic principles.

Soon after it seized power, the Taliban imposed an indefinite ban on girls' education beyond the sixth grade and, a few months later, also banned higher education for women until "further notice."

Women also were banned from entering gyms, parks and public baths, from taking part in sports and traveling to distant locations without a "mahram," or male guardian.

Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid has repeatedly said the administration is working to establish conditions under which girls and women can attend classrooms or university campuses in line with Islamic Sharia laws. The restrictions, nevertheless, remain in force.

While the U.N. has acknowledged that the country has become more stable since the takeover, it has warned that lasting stability cannot be possible unless the Taliban rulers — who remain isolated internationally — lift restrictions on women and girls, protect basic rights and address terrorism concerns.

"A reduction in conflict has brought tangible benefits for many Afghans and created opportunities to focus on recovery, development and regional economic cooperation," the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, or UNAMA, said in a statement ahead of the anniversary. It added, however, that the restrictions on women and girls impede Afghanistan's recovery and its reintegration with the international community.

In a statement this week, the U.N.'s agency on women's rights, said Afghan women and girls are living under the world's most severe restrictions, which not only violate their rights but also threaten the country's social and economic future.

"Half a decade after the Taliban takeover in August 2021, Afghanistan has systematically dismantled the rights of half its population, making it a global outlier with no parallel in the modern world," U.N. Women said.

"In the past year alone, this exclusion of women and girls from education, employment, public life, justice systems and healthcare has only intensified, entrenching what remains the world's most severe women's rights crisis," it said.

Fazila Soroush, a 39-year-old Kabul-based entrepreneur and an advocate for women's rights, said the government had "demonstrated its worth to the people through its actions in every area."

"We consider it essential that the officials of the Islamic Emirate who had announced the closure of schools and universities until further notice, now make a clear and practical decision regarding this matter," she said.

In the streets of Kabul, preparations for the anniversary celebrations were underway. Vendors sold the Taliban's white with black scripted flags while painters were busy writing slogans in praise of Islamic laws on walls, including: "The Islamic system has been achieved at the cost of the martyrs' blood" and "Our commitment stands firm: Consolidation and implementation of Islamic Sharia."

Molvi Hayatullah Mahajar Farahi, deputy minister in the Taliban government for broadcasting at the Ministry of Information and culture, said in the five years the administration has delivered security, stabilized the currency, improved infrastructure and formed industrial parks that have created jobs.

"Naturally, challenges and difficulties exist, yet we can highlight several accomplishments," Farahi told The Associated Press.

Farahi, when asked, did not address the issue of the education of girls and women but said "the level of investment made in universities surpasses anything seen in the past.

"The Emirate continues its efforts to further organize and improve services for our citizens in the fields of education and other sectors," he stated.

The deputy minister rejected a U.N. report that documented terrorist networks in Afghanistan, saying "these are merely enemy propaganda, spread to portray the country as unstable."

Asked to comment about its international isolation, Farahi insisted the Taliban government was engaged with some 40 countries. The Taliban government currently is only formally recognized by Russia.

"The Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan has fulfilled all the requirements necessary for official recognition. It is now up to the international community and others to step forward and take the appropriate action," he said.

The bans have left an estimated 2.4 million girls excluded from secondary education, UNESCO, the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, said this week — a 200,000 increase from last year. The restrictions have reversed two decades of progress that Afghanistan had made in education, the agency said.

Pointing at a broader educational crisis, the agency said 53% of primary school-aged children are out of school. Schools lack basic infrastructure such as water, sanitation or heating, while natural disasters have also led to hundreds of school closures.

Meanwhile, the U.N. World Food Program said child malnutrition has reached critical levels in a third of Afghanistan's provinces and is expected to worsen as funding shortfalls force cuts in food distributions and other support.

In Kabul, Dost Mohammad Khan expressed support for the Taliban administration, saying the past five years have brought stability. He said however, that the country needs trained professionals such as doctors and engineers, urging the authorities to keep "all sectors operational."

"We also call upon the Islamic Emirate to permit women to attend school under the sharia dress code and we urge the public to heed the directives of the Emirate also," said the 38-year-old.

Fraser reported from Ankara, Turkey.

title: This anti-war politician just fled Russia. He believes Putin knows the war is costing him support
description: Boris Nadezhdin has been in France just over a week, still reeling from his hasty exit from Russia after a sudden summons from its powerful Investigative Committee.
fullText:
Boris Nadezhdin struck a tired, yet still upbeat figure when we met on a blisteringly hot day in Paris. He'd been in France just over a week, still reeling from his hasty exit from Russia after a sudden summons from Russia's powerful Investigative Committee on what he assumed would be criminal charges.

After 40 years in Russian politics, he said he'd realized it was "a question of three days" before he might not have the choice to leave. "Normally, after you go to this place, you will receive the criminal paper and go to the court, and after court, go to jail: Lefortovo," he explained, referring to Moscow's most notorious prison, known for its brutal treatment of dissidents and political prisoners.

He checked his phone several times during the interview for updates from his lawyers.

He left his family in Russia, and on the day we met he missed his daughter's wedding. But he's managing to stay positive. "The good news is, I am alive and I am free," he said.

Many other opposition figures in President Vladimir Putin's Russia have been less fortunate.

Just a month ago, Nadezhdin was running a campaign for Russian parliamentary elections in September. Then came a short but brutal series of interventions by the authorities.

First, on July 10, he was declared a "foreign agent," a designation that, among many other restrictions, meant he wouldn't be able to serve in parliament. When he announced that he would continue campaigning regardless, he found himself arrested on an administrative charge – accused of displaying extremist symbols, a claim he described as ridiculous. On July 17, he received a small fine.

A day earlier, he had received a message on his government services account – an online portal Russians use for everything from healthcare to speeding fines – that he had been banned from leaving the country.

Three days later, the summons arrived from the Investigative Committee, Russia's top law-enforcement body, and the day after that, he says, the ban on leaving Russia "disappeared" from his online account. He believes this may have been a deliberate signal, and it enabled him to travel without being challenged.

"When the Kremlin administration want that opposition politician… to leave the country, number one they give him the criminal investigation… and second, they open the way to leave Russia."

Nadezhdin, an academic and former member of parliament in Russia in the early 2000s, and until recently a municipal lawmaker in his hometown of Dolgoprudny, just outside Moscow, had gained international fame when he attempted to challenge Putin in the 2024 presidential election, running on a manifesto that described the war in Ukraine as a "fatal mistake."

His effort to gather the required 100,000 signatures sparked an outpouring of public support, with people lining up outside his campaign offices in cities across Russia and beyond in a rare burst of organized dissent in a country that continues to systematically stamp out political opposition.

In the end, he was barred from running when Russian election authorities ruled that enough of the signatures he'd collected were invalid to put him below the threshold.

But despite increasing obstacles, including a bankruptcy case against him that led, he says, to the loss of his home, he pushed on, driven by the sense that more and more Russians were getting behind his anti-war message.

"We have found from the beginning of this year the deep changes in public opinion in Russia," he said. "Everybody wants to stop the war. It's in the society, it's in the elite and in the nearest people around Putin. And of course, the understanding of what this war really means for Russian economy, for Russian cities."

At the same time, strikingly in a country where state media has instilled in Russians the idea that Ukraine and the West are to blame for the war, Putin's approval rating is also dropping (albeit from a high level), according to various Russian polling organizations.

Nadezhdin believes those around Putin, and the Russian president himself, understand that "the only way to return the big support of people now… is to stop the war."

When and how that understanding translates into action, he doesn't know, and he's not optimistic about a durable settlement.

"It's quite possible to freeze the future strikes, mutual strikes. But the question of how to be in peace with West, be in peace with Ukraine, it's a question of next generations."

In the face of declining approval ratings, the Kremlin is reverting to more repressive tactics. Just this week, Russia's supreme court blocked Yabloko, the only remaining liberal, anti-war party on the ballot for parliamentary elections, from running. Dozens of young Russians gathered outside the court in solidarity as the decision came in.

"The political system has exposed itself," wrote Yabloko co-founder Grigory Yavlinsky on his Telegram channel. "It's clear, the desire for peace and freedom turned out to be much stronger than the authorities had thought."

Yabloko, which dates back to the early 1990s, has survived about as long in Russian politics as Nadezhdin, each weathering brutal pressure tactics, but allowed to remain as long as they didn't gain too much support. Nadezhdin's ouster now is all the more notable because he had tried to stick to the rules.

"I am not the strong enemy of the system like Nemtsov or like Navalny," he told CNN, referring to two of Putin's most charismatic opponents: Boris Nemtsov, who was gunned down near the Kremlin in 2015, and Aleksey Navalny, who died in a remote Russian penal colony in 2024.

"I didn't cross the red lines for 40 years of my political biography and 20 years, 25 years practically in opposition. I was integrated in the Russian political system," Nadezhdin said.

Those red lines were, he believed, never criticizing Putin personally (though he did criticize his policies, in particular the war in Ukraine) and never accepting funding from abroad.

"The red lines have changed and now, in Russia, it's absolutely impossible to criticize war."

title: ‘I feel like I’m at war’: are we losing the battle against machine-made music?
description:
Despite outcry from musicians, AI slop is creeping into the charts as record labels scramble to adapt to a new normal where hits can be made at the click of a button
This year, the battle for song of the summer has been eclipsed by a much more complicated – some would even say disturbing – debate. That’s because we find ourselves asking not “What’s the song of the summer?” but rather “Is the song of the summer even real?”
Among the top contenders for the title is Fenix Flexin’s Rubberz, a single released in June that has ascended to No 58 on the Billboard Hot 100 and racked up more than 35m Spotify streams. It’s not the sort of fare Fenix usually cooks up.
fullText:
This year, the battle for song of the summer has been eclipsed by a much more complicated – some would even say disturbing – debate. That’s because we find ourselves asking not “What’s the song of the summer?” but rather “Is the song of the summer even real?”

Among the top contenders for the title is Fenix Flexin’s Rubberz, a single released in June that has ascended to No 58 on the Billboard Hot 100 and racked up more than 35m Spotify streams. It’s not the sort of fare Fenix usually cooks up. The artist is known for his trap music as part of the rap duo Shoreline Mafia, but Rubberz is a mildly noirish, 80s-inspired synth-pop track featuring a voice nothing like his. The song has drawn comparisons to Morrissey, but it more closely resembles Men at Work’s Down Under, or a Weird Al Yankovic parody of Men at Work. It’s pretty awful. But more importantly, it has an uncanny quality to it. It sounds off.

Almost immediately after it came out, skeptics accused Fenix of employing artificial intelligence to create the track, if not entirely at least partly. He and the song’s credited producer, Purps on the Beat, initially denied it, with Fenix insisting that he’d just used Auto-Tune and a phoney British accent. The kerfuffle culminated this month when indie DJ-producer Medasin posted a video that he said proved that Rubberz had been made using the free generative music tool Treblo.

Medasin then captured himself giving Treblo prompts to pump out his own track. Its sound and lyrics were eerily close to those of Rubberz. Fenix rejected Medasin’s claims, posting what he said were clips of the song’s stems, or its fundamental components, but then Medasin posted a rebuttal of him demonstrating how AI songs, too, can be broken down into stems. A few days later, Fenix finally admitted to using AI to make Rubberz, writing: “never said I didn’t use AI, i said it had nun to do w recording process.”

This is in line with the findings of the platform’s own open-source classifier, Was This Made With Treblo?, which finds Rubberz to be “very likely Treblo” according to Wired. The tool hasn’t been independently reviewed, but the Treblo co-founder Ryan Tremblay confirmed to the Guardian that the classifier returns a very high probability score (“higher by far than any false positive”) for Rubberz, indicating that Treblo generated the song. “We built Treblo for everyone, from normal people experimenting at home to charting artists looking for new sounds,” Tremblay said. “Some artists appear to have used our model to find a sound that millions of people connected with, and that’s exciting.” When reached by the Guardian, Fenix’s representative declined to comment.

The uproar over Rubberz coincided with another major development in music in recent weeks. On 29 July, several record companies, including “the big three” – Universal Music Group, Sony Music and Warner Music Group – issued a proposal calling for global music charts to disqualify AI-generated tracks from consideration if they did not meet certain criteria. According to their suggested guidelines, a song could enter the charts only if it was properly authorized, lawful and substantially human-made, and does not raise concerns of streaming or chart manipulation. The issue, as the record companies stated in a press release, is that a significant number of AI-generated tracks hitting streaming services like Spotify have used tools trained on artists’ music without their consent and are often linked to fraudulently boosted streaming numbers. Under the proposed rules, these songs would not be allowed to enter charts such as the Billboard Hot 100.

At the same time, all the major record labels have announced partnerships with the likes of Nvidia, Spotify and Stability AI to develop AI music tools, with BMG announcing a partnership with the AI music-creation platform Suno this week. The rapper Tyga, a labelmate of Fenix, proudly told Vibe magazine recently that his new album $tarface was created with AI, saying: “There’s nothing wrong with using technology as a tool.” (The album received Pitchfork’s first 0.0 review in nearly two decades.)

He is not alone in his permissive attitude. While Rubberz is the first AI-generated single to crack the Hot 100, it is not the first to land on the Billboard charts. In November, the AI act Breaking Rust hit No 1 on the country digital song sales chart with Walk My Walk, a track credited to a person who goes by Aubierre Rivaldo Taylor. That same month, the AI-powered R&B singer Xania Monet – whose name instantly conjures actual human R&B singers Victoria Monét and Janelle Monáe – became the first AI act to enter a Billboard radio airplay chart, later climbing to No 1 on the R&B digital song sales chart. An avatar that the Mississippi poet Telisha “Nikki” Jones invented with Suno, she reportedly landed a multimillion-dollar record deal last fall.

After Xania Monet’s milestone, Billboard reported that a total of at least six AI-generated or AI-assisted artists had debuted on its various charts in 2025. The publication admitted, however, that the tally could be higher because it has become harder and harder to determine which songs have used AI, and just how much. This was validated a week later when a study by the French streaming platform Deezer and research firm Ipsos revealed that 97% of its participants couldn’t tell the difference between AI-generated music and human-made music.

Unsurprisingly, the proliferation of AI artists has struck a nerve with the human ones. SZA told i-D: “I feel like I’m at war because of AI.” Last month, she slammed AI generators like Suno and alleged that they were being trained on her songs without her permission. “If you’re a musician and you support this degenerate shit? You’re disgusting and there’s nothing you could ever say to me to make this OK,” she said. Jack Antonoff recently called AI-music makers “godless whores”. Billie Eilish, Bad Bunny, Kate Bush, Annie Lennox, Nick Cave, Sting, Stevie Wonder and Paul McCartney have all protested against the heavy use of generative AI in music.

And why shouldn’t they? Yes, dictating what one wants to create to an app requires a sliver of inspiration and imagination, but it pales in comparison with the blood, sweat and tears artists pour into music of their own – music that hasn’t been trained, often without permission, on reams of pre-existing copyrighted work. If those artists’ labor is grueling, the results, performed live and perfected in a studio by bands and session players with real instruments, can be deeply moving and totally exhilarating. Directing prompts to AI music generators like Suno, Udio and Treblo to spit out fully formed songs for mass consumption is a faster, cheaper, easier way to make music. It also disrespects and debases the art form, reducing hard-earned craft to half-assed mimicry.

If the outcry against AI sounds like a bunch of intransigent luddites shaking their fists at the inevitable arrival of a new era, know that naysaying artists and wary record companies are not alone. A recent report published by the music and entertainment insights company Luminate showed that listeners, especially members of gen Z and gen Alpha, are increasingly uneasy with AI-generated songs. The study found that 44% of US respondents felt less inclined to listen to a song if it involves generative AI. “Consumers are net negative,” a Luminate analyst told NPR in May. “People are more likely to feel uncomfortable than to feel comfortable with AI use.”

Universal, Sony and Warner are not demanding an outright ban on AI music from charts and streaming services. Though all three sued the AI music generators Suno and Udio in 2024, alleging they had trained their platforms on the labels’ artists without their permission, Universal settled with Udio and Warner settled with both Suno and Udio last year. (Sony has yet to settle with either.) The labels continue to work with Spotify and AI companies to develop generative music tools, in a move that effectively keeps their options open. Warner executive Robert Kyncl said the deals would foster “new creative and commercial possibilities”, adding: “Now, we are entering the next phase of innovation. The democratization of music creation.” Universal, Sony and Warner did not respond when approached by the Guardian for comment.

Meanwhile, other artists have expressed support of AI as a means to enhance songwriting. “With new technology, I try to use it as a tool to grow, not a crutch,” Björk wrote in a 2025 post on X. “If there is no soul in tomorrow’s music made by AI, it is because no one put it there … Anything that is mass-manufactured without the attention of creativity is that way, AI or not. So it is not about the tool – it is what you do with it.” Even McCartney enlisted AI to isolate John Lennon’s vocals for the final Beatles song, 2023’s Now and Then. What these labels and so many musicians want is a system of guardrails to ensure that AI use is limited, honest and transparent.

There is hope. In January, Bandcamp banned all music fully or substantially created by AI from the platform. Though Tidal allows fully AI-generated songs on its app if they are not linked to fraud or artist impersonation, they cannot collect streaming royalties or direct-to-fan sales revenue, and get tagged with an “AI” label. A coalition of music industry organizations, including the Grammys and the Recording Industry Association of America, recently announced that it was taking steps to notify listeners of AI use in recordings. This month, Spotify said that it would label AI artists with an “AI Persona” tag and exclude these artists from its personalized recommendations, while its optional “AI Credits” feature allows artists to note whether AI was used in a song’s creation.

Per the record companies’ proposed criteria, such AI Personas would not be chart-eligible. If Deezer’s findings are any indication, plenty of listeners would support this. Its 2025 survey results showed that 80% of respondents agreed that entirely AI-generated music should be clearly labeled to listeners, while 52% thought entirely AI-generated songs should not be included alongside human-made songs in the main charts.

Author and journalist CJ Farley echoed this sentiment in a recent column for Time. He dismissed the terms “AI artists” and “AI musicians”, suggesting that we instead refer to AI releases as “AI products”. Then he took it a step further, arguing that these products should be confined to their own chart “away from human musicians with real lives and with real financial obligations”.

If Rubberz is a joke, Fenix Flexin might have been trying to see exactly how much he could get away with. (That would at least explain why the song is such dreck.) But what about all the AI products with more nefarious purposes floating around out there undetected, the slop created by impostors and opportunists attempting to steal the work of others and pass it off as their own? There’s more at stake here than chart rankings. Artists’ livelihoods and legacies are on the line. If we don’t act now, tomorrow’s song of the summer may just be a sad, hollow shell of yesterday’s.

title: Ukrainian drones wipe out US tank brigade in live war game
description: Ukrainian drone pilots teach the US military and NATO hard battlefield lessons.
fullText:
Ukrainian drone teams demolished a brigade of US Army tanks and armored vehicles during a live war game held this year—but the US soldiers were lucky enough to get “respawn” attempts while learning from the experience.

The semiannual military exercise, called Combined Resolve, gave the US military a firsthand taste of how modern drone warfare has evolved on the battlefields of Ukraine. The Ukrainian drone operators participating in the exercise were easily able to spot and destroy US armored vehicles by mimicking the actions of dropping bombs from above or moving close enough to simulate a kamikaze strike, according to US officials and a participant who spoke with The Wall Street Journal.

US armored vehicles were being destroyed so quickly that they were “respawned” and sent back into the simulated fray, a US official told The Wall Street Journal. The US troops who participated in the exercise—held in Germany from April 9 to May 10—were on rotational deployment from Fort Hood, Texas.

“Using the drones with the Army, it keeps everyone on edge,” according to an unidentified US Army soldier in a promotional video for Combined Resolve. “There is never a safe spot or safe moment in the game anymore.”

The participating troops hailed from the 3rd Armored Brigade Combat Team of the 1st Cavalry Division, which typically operates armored vehicles, like M1A2 tanks and Bradley infantry fighting vehicles.

But by repeating the training scenario throughout the two-week exercise, US Army troops got better at figuring out how to disperse and hide from the drones while using countermeasures such as electronic warfare.

The US military is not alone in learning such lessons from battle-hardened Ukrainian drone operators.

Ukrainian drone teams also participated in a Swedish-led military exercise for NATO, called Aurora 26, that was also held in May. A mock mechanized assault by NATO tanks and infantry fighting vehicles allowed Ukrainian drones to take out dozens of the attacking armored vehicles, which eventually forced planners to reset the war game, The Kyiv Independent reported.

Armored tanks first played a useful role in helping break through entrenched battlefield lines during the final years of World War I more than a century ago. But since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, frontline combat has seen the return of positional warfare centered on fortified networks of trenches. That is because the increased lethality of modern drone warfare has largely negated large assaults by armored vehicles and troops in recent years.

The current lethality of the so-called drone kill zone has forced both sides to rely primarily on infiltration tactics using small groups or even individual soldiers when trying to take or reclaim territory, sometimes riding motorcycles, all-terrain vehicles, or horses. Russia’s offensives, which are aimed at seizing more Ukrainian territory, have been reduced to bloody attritional operations where soldiers are sent forward on near-suicidal missions in what Russians themselves describe as the “meat grinder.”

Meanwhile, armored tanks and vehicles have mostly become an endangered species on the frontlines. Russia has lost more than 14,000 tanks and armored vehicles of other types during the war, according to the Dutch open source intelligence tracking project Oryx, which only counted visually verified losses. Ukraine has lost over 6,000 armored combat vehicles.

But both Russia and Ukraine are still attempting to use mechanized assaults with vehicles on occasion. In May of this year, Ukraine used armored vehicles in limited counterattacks that penetrated Russian defenses—the result of Ukrainian military experiments with using electronic warfare and targeted strikes on Russian drone pilots to help achieve localized territorial gains. That was a notable feat, given that enabling mechanized vehicles to survive the Russian drone kill zone was “categorically impossible in 2025,” according to the Institute for the Study of War based in Washington, DC.

In July, Russian forces launched their own mechanized assault with tanks and infantry fighting vehicles in the hotly contested Donetsk Oblast in eastern Ukraine. This attack was apparently repelled, with the Ukrainian military reportedly destroying 80 percent of the Russian vehicles before they even reached the frontlines.

The Pentagon has requested more than $54 billion for acquiring drone and counterdrone systems in its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal, an amount that exceeds Ukraine’s entire military budget. But as the Combined Resolve exercise showed, the US military must also adapt its unit training and operational practices to the threat of short-range drones if it wants troops to survive on future battlefields.

title: Peggy Flanagan vows to 'rip ICE apart' after toppling moderate Dem in key Senate battle
description: Peggy Flanagan defeated Angie Craig in Minnesota's Democratic primary, backed by Bernie Sanders and Ilhan Omar in a growing progressive proxy war.
fullText:
Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, who scored an impressive win in Minnesota's Democratic primary for Senate, wants to blow up Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after two slayings rattled her state earlier this year. 

"Now let's talk about Donald Trump's out of control ICE force," Flanagan said during her victory speech Tuesday night. "We need to rip ICE apart and stop them from terrorizing our communities. And I know this. I know that we can fix our broken immigration system, secure the border, and create a real pathway to citizenship that aligns with our values."

Flanagan is another progressive insurgent challenging the status quo in the Democratic Party and handed Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., another defeat in the progressive proxy war in her decisive victory over Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn.

Republicans Get The Democrat They Wanted As Socialist Abdul El-sayed Wins Michigan Senate Primary

Flanagan, like other progressives in the hunt for a position of power in Congress, has honed her left-leaning bona fides by backing Medicare for all and pushing an end to military aid to Israel.

She's vowed to go after ICE on the campaign trail in the wake of the two deadly immigration enforcement-related shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota, and used Craig's support of legislation, like the Laken Riley Act, as a political cudgel to build a distinction between the two of them.

Those positions have earned her the backing of progressive heavyweights like Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and even Sen. Tina Smith, D-Minn., whose decision to retire from the Senate opened up the contest. 

Notably, Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., who is running for governor, has not weighed in on the race so far.

Craig, who was viewed as the safer, more moderate pick, had the backing of the Democratic old-guard, including Schumer.

Big Money Propels Dem Megachurch Pastor To Victory In Longshot Kansas Senate Bid

Republicans are licking their chops, too, at Schumer getting handed another loss.

"Morale among Chuck Schumer's establishment is at an all-time low, and Bernie Sanders' socialist flank is filling the gap with candidates like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed," Bernadette Breslin, a spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told Fox News Digital.

And it's also brought reams of cash into the race. Craig has raised nearly $13 million this cycle, according to filings from the Federal Election Commission, while Flanagan has raked in just shy of $7 million.

"Peggy Flanagan is about bringing about real change, standing up to the big money interests," Sanders told "Face the Nation" on Sunday. "There is a reason why the super PACs and the billionaires are flooding Minnesota with all kinds of money. Same thing as Michigan."

Republicans see Flanagan's candidacy in the same vein as Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, who last week similarly squeaked out a narrow win over Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., who, like Craig, has Schumer's backing.

Bomb-thrower Dem Makes Shocking Promise To Kick Schumer To Curb During Senate Debate

They also have built-in messaging against her: Flanagan was Walz's right hand as the Minnesota fraud scandal rippled across the airwaves and nation. While the scandal killed his prospects of running for reelection as governor, it has so far not kneecapped Flanagan's candidacy. And Walz hasn't waded into the endorsement game in the Senate contest, either.

They're confident that national Republicans' candidate of choice, former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya, will be the one to turn Minnesota red. There's also the possibility that Flanagan, who has not raked in the same level of cash that Craig did, may become a resource drain for other key races on Democrats' scorecard.

"Minnesota and Michigan being in play was not on Chuck Schumer's bingo card this cycle," a GOP operative told Fox News Digital. "It remains to be seen which battleground(s) Democrats will have to pull resources from to drag socialists like Peggy Flanagan and Abdul El-Sayed across the finish line in November."

And Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., when asked by CNN which races kept him up at night, said one contest gave him hope.

"The one thing that gets me excited when I think about this election cycle on the map is Minnesota," said Scott, the chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC). "I think Minnesota, we have a real shot with Michele Tafoya."

"What we know without question is, she is within a point of the lieutenant governor right now," he said. "So if we can continue to let her show the contrast between the two candidates, I think Michele Tafoya's the kind of Republican that can win."

title: Zelenskiy: Ukraine has given US negotiators proposals for ending the war with Russia
description: Aug 11 () - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had handed proposals to U. negotiators for a plan to end the war with Moscow and suggested that Russia ‌would use its parliamenta...
fullText:
Aug 11 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukraine had handed proposals to U.S. negotiators for a plan to end the war with Moscow and suggested that Russia ‌would use its parliamentary election next month as a pretext to declare a new mobilisation.

Zelenskiy's announcement ‌of fresh proposals for peace talks, largely stalled since the outbreak of the conflict with Iran, comes amid suggestions by both ​Russia and Ukraine that U.S. negotiators would soon pay a visit to their two countries.

"We have conveyed our proposals to the American side," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address.

"And the United States can help strengthen our defence, first and foremost with air defence, and put pressure on Russia so that its plans are different -- to ‌prepare for an end to the war ⁠rather than prolonging it."

Zelenskiy offered no details on the proposals.

U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were last in Moscow last January and have not yet visited Kyiv.

Ukraine ⁠has repeatedly called for a ceasefire after nearly 4-1/2 years of fighting. Russia says it wants a settlement, but any solution must involve Ukraine fully ceding four regions Moscow claims as well as resolving the conflict's "root causes."

In his ​remarks, ​Zelenskiy said Ukrainian intelligence had evidence that Russia would exploit ​its September "pseudo-election" -- a reference to restrictions imposed ‌on the polls -- to proclaim a new mobilisation to boost the numbers of fighting personnel.

"They are preparing for mobilisation in the autumn, immediately after the imitation of parliamentary elections," Zelenskiy said as part of a plan to "create the appearance that Russians supposedly support the war."

"Then, following the so-called election, he plans an additional rapid mobilisation of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, plus another similar number next year."

The ‌draft, he said, would be in addition to recruitment through ​the conclusion of contracts with servicemen.

The Putin-backed United Russia Party ​and other broadly pro-Kremlin parties are set to ​retain their dominance in the Russian parliament after the vote.

Russia's Supreme Court on Monday ‌barred the liberal Yabloko party, the only officially ​registered party that opposes ​Moscow's war in Ukraine, from competing in the election.

Russia declared a "partial mobilisation" in 2022 after the launch in February of its full-scale invasion. Zelenskiy has previously suggested that Moscow would introduce a new ​mobilisation.

Russian officials have declined to discuss ‌the issue.

Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, one of Russia's most ardent hawks, said last month ​that Russia needed no new mobilisation as 200,000 volunteers had signed contracts in the first ​half of 2026.

title: Carcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughs
description:
After the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twist
‘Claustrophobic”, “oppressive”, “pretty depressing” – these are the words Jeffrey Tomec and Dave van Egdom volunteer when I ask them to reflect on their work as part of Swedish indie developer Wrong Organ. I’d add “nightmare-inducing”, too. Their last game, Mouthwashing, was an acclaimed work of horror storytelling set on a scuttled space freighter, in which players uncover the horrible things its desperate crew have done to each other.
When you’re planning a follow-up to something so pitilessly nasty, how do you raise the stakes? fullText:
After the success of space horror Mouthwashing, Swedish developer Wrong Organ has created a Battlefield-inspired co-op with a supernatural twist

‘Claustrophobic”, “oppressive”, “pretty depressing” – these are the words Jeffrey Tomec and Dave van Egdom volunteer when I ask them to reflect on their work as part of Swedish indie developer Wrong Organ. I’d add “nightmare-inducing”, too. Their last game, Mouthwashing, was an acclaimed work of horror storytelling set on a scuttled space freighter, in which players uncover the horrible things its desperate crew have done to each other.

When you’re planning a follow-up to something so pitilessly nasty, how do you raise the stakes? Well, you could set the entire game in the stifling crew compartment of a heavily armoured tank, a coffin-like interior you share with two other players as you co-operatively attempt to pilot your beleaguered war machine to safety through the crumbling remains of a city in enemy territory.

While there’s undoubtedly tonal overlap, the roaring engine powering Carcass Clad is gameplay rather than scriptwriting. “In Mouthwashing, every single thing we were doing was about trying to make that script come to life in any way possible,” says Tomec, the gameplay lead. “Every gameplay sequence, everything you do at every point is just there to make that story hit. And Carcass Clad is fundamentally not that kind of game. This is a gameplay-driven experience.”

That gameplay is physical, tactile and always high pressure, whether you choose to play as a gunner, driver or commander. “You’re surrounded by this awesome but scary machinery,” says technical designer and self-described tank nerd Van Egdom. “It should feel as though you might lose a finger if you put your hand in the wrong place.” And you will put a hand wrong at some point, since each role is designed so that your attention is stretched to breaking point between urgent competing priorities. One crewmate’s foul-up can have cascading effects for the entire crew.

If all that sounds a bit, well, claustrophobic, oppressive and depressing, it isn’t even the worst part. Your adversaries aren’t run-of-the-mill camo-clad baddies. No – your lone crew is pursued through Vhorgorod by the last remnants of the broken city’s defenders, the most dogged and fanatical element of the military force once stationed here. It’s a dynamic that was inspired in part by Battlefield V – specifically one mission that casts you as the crew of a German Tiger tank still defending Cologne in March 1945.

Vhorgorod’s defenders, the Green Lions, hunt you through wreckage and ruins. Tomec hints that their supernatural dabblings have “unleashed something on the city”, and now strange growths of flesh and gold fester alongside the rubble and debris. If that’s not grisly enough, the Green Lions’ tanks are festooned with divine livestock, living armour that moos and grunts and bleeds as shells fly.

But for all that horror, Carcass Clad is a co-op game, which means that it is also, on occasion, a bit funny. For all the grimness and tension, players are still going to be laughing when the driver inadvertently slams the Yksiö tank into reverse at a critical moment.

“When you’re designing a co-op game, you’re trying to take into account the fact that every co-op game is inherently a silly game,” says Tomec. “We want – both narratively and at the gameplay level – the feeling that you’re a team fighting against these very oppressive odds, coming together and still finding revelry and enjoyment in being able to overcome something that is pretty miserable.”

On some level, that might be the biggest difference between Mouthwashing and Carcass Clad: a belief that in spite of everything, people can hold together, work together and even find something to smile about.

title: Ousted Syrian dictator Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
description: The ex-president is convicted of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.
fullText:
A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.

It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to Moscow with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power.

Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He had been put on trial and appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence.

Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule.

In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces.

That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.

Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year.

Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.

He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death".

The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell.

The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij.

Nouha al-Masri has spent 15 years waiting for this moment.

She is not just part of the five person prosecution team, she is also a plaintiff in this case.

Masri lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at Al-Omari Square in Deraa.

"The verdict reflects the magnitude of the sacrifices we made, the sacrifices of the martyrs, the suffering and pain of the victims, the missing, and the detainees," she told the BBC.

"We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us."

For Masri, the verdict is a new chapter.

"Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."

Syria trial seen as first step on long road for Assad's victims

The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding

Calls for justice and accountability in Syria grow after Assad's fall

It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow.

It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership.

An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture.

He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty.

Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia.

Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions.

Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994.

Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies.

Much of his rule was defined by the civil war.

Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus.

title: Iran installs new war chiefs as Tehran signals ‘prolonged confrontation,’ expert warns
description: Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei named six military commanders as an expert says Tehran is preparing for prolonged confrontation, not settlement.
fullText:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei formally appointed six senior military commanders Monday, cementing a wartime reshuffle as Tehran rebuilds a command structure impacted by months of U.S. and Israeli strikes.

The appointments, announced by Khamenei's office and promoted on social media, fill posts across Iran's armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij paramilitary force, with a counterterrorism expert warning the timing and language of the decrees signal Tehran is preparing for "prolonged confrontation" and not a settlement with Washington.

"Strategically, the announcements made were issued in English, on X, while Iranian and Omani negotiators finalize the coordinates of a proposed shipping route through Hormuz, which is deliberate sequencing," Dr. Omar Mohammed, director of the Antisemitism Research Initiative at George Washington University's Program on Extremism, told Fox News Digital.

"Tehran is establishing its command structure as a fact on the ground before it signs anything."

Trump Says Iran Will Pay — What It Takes To End The War Remains Unclear

Mohammed also pointed to language in the appointment announcements blaming the deaths of predecessors on what Iran called the "Zionist-American enemy."

"That phrase, in formal state documents, codifies the United States as a co-belligerent," Mohammed said.

Khamenei appointed Ali Abdollahi as chief of staff of the armed forces and Kioumars Heydari as his deputy. He also formally named Ahmad Vahidi commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, promoting him to the rank of major general.

Mostafa Izadi was named deputy IRGC commander, Ali Azmaei as commander of the IRGC Navy and Hossein Taeb as commander of the Basij.

Mohammed said Vahidi was also instructed to maintain readiness for "powerful offensive operations against the enemy," by the Supreme Leader, while Abdollahi was tasked with completing the integration of the General Staff into the Khatam al-Anbiya wartime joint command.

"States exiting a conflict dismantle their wartime command arrangements, but Iran is now institutionalizing its own," Mohammed said. "The decrees here describe a leadership planning for a prolonged confrontation, not a settlement."

Several of the newly appointed commanders have previously faced U.S. or European sanctions or allegations tied to terrorism and violent crackdowns.

Vahidi is the subject of an Interpol Red Notice requested by Argentina over his alleged involvement in the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people.

Taeb, a former chief of the IRGC Intelligence Organization and former Basij commander, is on the U.S. Treasury Department's sanctions list.

The United States first designated him in 2010 over serious human rights abuses following Iran's disputed 2009 presidential election.

Heydari was also sanctioned by the United States in 2022 after the Treasury Department said he had publicly acknowledged his forces' involvement in the violent response to Iran's November 2019 protests, in which hundreds of protesters were killed.

The European Union has also sanctioned him.

Iran's Unseen Supreme Leader Becomes Weapon In Escalating Power Struggle, Experts Say

The reshuffle comes as Iran continues rebuilding its political and military leadership after a series of U.S. and Israeli strikes killed senior figures across the regime.

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had served as supreme leader since 1989, was killed in a Feb. 28 strike at the start of the war. Mojtaba Khamenei, was selected as Iran's new supreme leader in March.

Ali Larijani, then secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a major figure in the country's security and foreign policy establishment, and Gholamreza Soleimani, commander of the Basij, were killed in strikes on March 17.

The latest appointments come amid continuing questions about Mojtaba Khamenei's health and public absence.

President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Monday that he had held a nearly seven-hour meeting with Khamenei, only the second meeting the president has publicly disclosed since the new supreme leader took office, Iran International reported.

Khamenei has not appeared publicly since being selected in March and is believed to have been wounded in the Feb. 28 strike that killed his father.

Pezeshkian said the two discussed economic conditions, sanctions and other domestic challenges and that Khamenei emphasized the need for "unity and cohesion."

The military rebuild, however, has not extended fully into Iran's sensitive intelligence apparatus, according to Mohammed.

"The IRGC Intelligence Organization and its counterintelligence arm have no announced chiefs, and Iran has no permanent defense or intelligence ministers," the expert said.

"The appointments require assigning responsibility for the counterintelligence failures that enabled the February decapitation.

"Whoever wins that argument — the supreme leader's circle or the Guard's institutional leadership — is the actor actually in control."

title: Trump pivots back to sanctions for Iran as other strategies to end his war fizzle
description: President Donald Trump likes to say that he started his war with Iran after 50 years of economic pressure had failed to stop its nuclear weapons ambitions — but he’s now betting that another financial...
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump likes to say that he started his war with Iran after 50 years of economic pressure had failed to stop its nuclear weapons ambitions — but he's now betting that another financial squeeze can bring an end to that war.

The Trump administration is hoping that months of bombing have pushed Iran's economy to a breaking point that will force its leadership to cave to demands to end its nuclear program and fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to oil and natural gas tankers.

The president on Monday said that since Iran is seeking compensation as part of any peace talks, he now intends to demand the same for the U.S. side. It's part of a larger pivot this weekend by Trump to argue that Iran is now on the cusp of financially collapsing, even though it has already endured decades of financial sanctions, which are often a longer-term strategy rather than an immediate tool of warfare that can halt a conflict.

The shift comes as U.S. stockpiles of key weapons have dwindled and as stop-start talks seem again to have stalled. But Trump insists the pressure can lead to a breakthrough.

"Yeah, they can make trouble, but they're broke," Trump told reporters. "They have no money. You know, Iran is broke, totally broke. And, they're not paying their soldiers. They have inflation of 300%."

Inflation is running high in Iran, although Trump's estimates were higher than what administration officials have been citing to reporters. But the prospect of a longer war also carries inflation risks for other nations, including the U.S. — where the war and higher gasoline prices are unpopular.

Crude oil prices climbed on Monday as investors interpreted Trump's comments as a sign that fewer ships would be traversing the Strait of Hormuz, continuing to limit global supplies of gasoline, jet fuel, natural gas and other forms of energy. The Iran war largely closed the waterway involved in shipping roughly 20% of global oil supplies before the conflict — and attempts to reopen the strait have been short-lived as it has become a source of leverage for the Iranians in negotiations.

Iran does not appear to be publicly intimidated by the prospect of more financial sanctions.

"Whenever Washington proves itself incapable of pursuing diplomacy, it retreats into sanctions; and whenever those sanctions fail to produce results, it simply increases the dose," said Esmaeil Baqaei, spokesman for Iran's Foreign Ministry, on social media. "The real risk is that American politicians, clinging to this bad habit, will instead strangle their own remaining chances of a less humiliating exit from a crisis of their own making."

The president didn't say what additional financial pressure would be applied, but the administration has since April 16 been engaged in what it calls " Operation Economic Fury " against Iran. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called this component the "financial equivalent" of a bombing campaign as the countries that buy oil from Iran or bank with it could be sanctioned.

But one problem with this pivot is that the sanctions are unable to bite as quickly as the impact of the largely shuttered strait, said Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University who helped direct Iran sanctions strategy in the Obama administration.

Nephew stressed that the value of sanctions as a tool is limited because Trump has not articulated clear strategic goals for the war, at times stressing that it can't have a nuclear weapon, then emphasizing the strait and then talking about ballistic missiles. Instead, Trump has engaged in a massive series of aerial assaults and a level of destruction that has not produced the quick end that he initially promised.

"Economic pressure is a possible element in his strategy, but he's yet to explain the purpose," Nephew said. "Trump has systematically weakened his own hand through his inadequate use of force, inarticulate elucidation of an objective, and vacillation on negotiations."

Still, the sanctions and the ongoing U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports give the U.S. economic and financial leverage, said Juan Zarate, a deputy national security adviser in the George W. Bush administration. Zarate said the U.S. sanctions threatening third-party countries doing business with Iran also have an impact. But these things take time, he noted.

"The ultimate question will be how far the United States is willing to go to constrict Iran's oil trade and threaten third countries with severe sanctions -- and whether it has the patience to test whether the economic pain will change the regime's behavior," Zarate said.

Trump's latest pivot to economic issues with Iran is something of a flip-flop. Trump has long derided past presidents who used sanctions to limit Iran's economic ability to pay for its military and nuclear development. In a speech last week in Las Vegas, he defended the bombing, missiles and drone attacks that began on Feb. 28 by indicating that the sanctions from previous administrations that date back to November 1979 had failed to succeed.

"It's been 47 years, but really, it's been 50 years because they've been saying 47 for three years, it's been 50 years," Trump said. "And no other president has done what you should have done a long time ago, because Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, can't have it."

The Iranian economy has suffered gravely because of the war, with the International Monetary Fund estimating the overall economy shrinks by 5.4% and the Iranian government recently reporting an annual inflation rate of 88.6%. The U.S. Treasury Department said average loadings of Iranian oil have decreased from 1.8 million barrels per day before the war to less than 500,000 barrels per day over the past month.

The U.S. economy — the world's largest — has continued to grow, but inflation is elevated and borrowing costs have risen in ways that have hurt Trump's popularity and led to disapproval of the Iran war.

A senior U.S. official, insisting on anonymity to discuss strategy, said the U.S. military has set back Iran's ability to produce, sell and ship oil and other energy resources. The administration sees the naval blockade of the strait and sanctions as effective and views Trump as having additional options that can be cranked harder in the weeks and months ahead.

Trump is essentially arguing that U.S. voters are better able to tolerate any economic inconveniences than Iranians, who have been in a state of economic hardship for years.

"It's not just what the military can do — we've got the most powerful economy in the world as well," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Monday in a joint appearance with Bessent. "And when you've got a motivated treasury secretary who can pull a lot of levers because he knows how to do it, you can put a lot of pressure on adversaries."

AP White House reporter Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

Israel has taken delivery of its most advanced and expensive submarine from Germany, expanding its fleet amid escalating regional threats, according to reports.

The handover of the INS Drakon is expected to significantly bolster Israel's underwater strike and reconnaissance capabilities, The Algemeiner reported. The warship had been scheduled to be delivered in 2025.

Trump Admin Pitches 15-Point Iran Peace Proposal As Pakistan Offers To Hold Talks

"Some of them would have to be at sea, on high alert, around the clock, if Iran suddenly attacked Israel in such a way that would cripple the IDF, including its strategic capabilities," Eilam said.

"In such a drastic scenario, Israel's submarine/s that would be at sea could respond," he added.

"Israel's other submarines might be in Haifa harbor at the time. They might be attacked and unable to operate. This demonstrates how important it is to always have submarines at sea."

TKMS reportedly handed over the INS Drakon—the sixth Dolphin-class vessel and third modified Dolphin II-class submarine in Israel's fleet—at its shipyard in Kiel, Germany, in late July.

Us Moves Airborne Troops, Marines As Iran Rejects Ceasefire, Raising Ground War Potential

Measuring more than 70 meters (230 feet) in length with a displacement exceeding 2,000 tons, the vessel is reported to be the largest submarine constructed in Germany since World War II, carrying an estimated price tag of $634 million, according to The Algemeiner.

According to Israeli outlet Ynet , Israel's Dolphin-class fleet also provides the nation with a critical sea-based second-strike capability in its defense program.

"Everything is going according to plan with the new program for Israel," TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard told Ynet Global.

"That also applies to the handover of the last boat of the previous series, including the homecoming in Israel," he said of the expansive submarine program.

The INS Drakon's arrival comes as Israel projects increasing military power across distant operational theaters, Eilam said.

Trump Is Proving That The Way To Better Our Military Is To Secure Our Supply Chains

"Israel has been acquiring submarines for several purposes. One of them is for deterrence and retribution, such as if Iran manages to develop nuclear weapons," Eilam said before adding that "Israel has to be ready."

While submarines on active deployment carry out intelligence and reconnaissance missions across the Mediterranean Sea, their primary objective remains readiness for "doomsday scenarios," Eilam noted.

"Israel's new submarine is bigger than others, which suggests Israel wants to have more options, such as increasing the range of the submarine's missiles so they can reach every target in Iran, even if the Israeli submarine is in the Mediterranean Sea," Eilam said.

"That way the submarine does not have to get closer to Iran, which requires crossing the Suez Canal, and this could be very risky, if not impossible in some situations," he added. "The other alternative is to bypass all of Africa, which would take a long time."

The new submarine was named INS Drakon (Dragon) — a mythical sea creature symbolizing strength, uniqueness and power — was chosen because it contains the Hebrew letters ד׳, ק׳, ר׳ (Dakar), thus commemorating the legacy of the submarine INS Dakar and its crew, the Ministry of Defense said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Israeli Navy, the Ministry of Defense, TKMS and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for comment.

title: Taiwan's war drills showcased a new strike drone class that Ukraine used to smash Russia this year
description: Taiwan's navy deployed two fixed-wing propeller drones, which officials described as "mid-size suicide drones" that were locally built.
fullText:
Taiwan showcased two midsize strike drones above its southwest coast on Saturday.

Their designs and descriptions draw easy comparisons to Ukraine's mid-range drones.

Such drones likely give Taiwan the ability to cheaply hit a Chinese invasion force over the horizon.

TSOYING, TAIWAN — Taiwan's navy deployed two medium-class strike drones on Saturday for the island's biggest annual military exercise, and their designs resemble those of the loitering munitions giving Ukraine fresh wins against Russia this year.

The pair of fixed-wing, propeller-driven drones appeared during a littoral combat drill simulating an attack on Tsoying, Taiwan's southwest coast.

It was the first time these drones were shown at the Han Kuang exercise, Taiwan's annual rehearsals against a Chinese invasion.

As the drones loitered for about 30 minutes above the beach, Taiwanese military officials described them to reporters as "medium-size suicide drones," adding they were locally built. The island's National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology designs and manufactures the vast majority of Taiwan's homegrown weapons.

"The drone used was provided by the Armament Bureau to the navy for testing purpose," a spokesperson for Taiwan's navy told Business Insider.

They declined to comment on the drone's specifications or whether its design was influenced in any way by the recent wars in Ukraine or the Middle East.

The one-way drones were not shown attempting to launch an attack, and it's unclear whether they represent Taiwan's final designs for the aircraft.

Ukraine has been using similar fixed-wing drones to attack Russian forces roughly 30 to 300 km behind the front lines this year, mainly disrupting supply routes that the Kremlin has relied on to funnel resources to the war.

Tsoying, where Taiwan hosts its largest naval base, is about 295 km, or 183 miles, from mainland China.

"The desire to employ more medium-range drones fits into things that Taiwan has learned from Ukraine," said Bryce Barros, a visiting fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, a Taipei think-tank backed by the Taiwanese government.

Mid-range drones would fill a gap in Taiwan's littoral defense with a cheaper way to strike Chinese forces or weapons from "over-the-horizon" as they approach the island, Barros said.

Unlike Ukraine's plains and forests, Taiwan's littoral defense covers a strait notorious for bad winds and volatile sea states, suggesting that Taipei may want its own drone built to withstand poor weather.

Instead of air defense systems or supply trucks like in Ukraine or Crimea, Taiwan's mid-range drones would likely target slow-moving vessels transporting troops or weapons, Barros added.

"A range of 40 kilometers to 60 kilometers would be very useful for a whole host of different platforms, anything to make it more difficult for the PLA to start getting into Taiwan's territorial waters," he said, referring to the People's Liberation Army.

Taiwan's government has said that it plans to produce 100,000 drones a month by 2030. In June, its national defense ministry proposed a $6.6 billion budget to procure over 210,000 domestically produced attack, reconnaissance, and sea drones.

It's all part of the island's emerging "hellscape" strategy, which aims to hamper Chinese forces attempting to cross the Taiwan Strait by flooding it with thousands of aerial, surface, and underwater drones.

The littoral drills on Saturday, attended by Taiwanese president Lai Ching-te, also featured naval special forces deploying in the island's homegrown M109 Skyship rigid-hull inflatable boats.
